questions.question: Two aircraft have the same CD0, and the second has twice the reference area. How does their parasite drag compare at the same dynamic pressure?
options: The second has twice the drag: its flat-plate area is doubled
They have the same drag: equal CD0 means equal drag
The second has half the drag: it is spread over more area
The second has four times the drag: it grows with area squared
questions.explanation: The flat-plate area f = CD0 Sref expresses the drag as an area, and the parasite drag is q f. A coefficient alone does not compare two aircraft of different size.

questions.question: In the SR22 build-up, with fully turbulent flow, the fuselage has Cf = 0.00246 and the wing 0.00322. Why is the fuselage value lower?
options: Its Reynolds number is higher, because Re uses its length
Its Mach correction is larger, because the fuselage is longer
Its flow stays laminar over more of its length than the wing's
Its shape is more slender, and Cf falls with slenderness
questions.explanation: Re = ρV l/μ uses the component length or chord: 22.42 ft for the fuselage against 3.98 ft for the wing. The turbulent Cf falls as Re rises.

questions.question: A wing is analyzed with transition at 40% of the chord, and in service insects and paint chips roughen it. What happens to its skin friction?
options: Transition moves forward and Cf rises toward the turbulent value
Transition moves aft and Cf falls toward the laminar value
Transition stays at 40% of the chord and only the form factor rises
Transition stays at 40% of the chord and Cf depends on Re only
questions.explanation: Insects and paint chips move transition forward, so more of the chord is turbulent and Cf climbs toward the fully turbulent value. The build-up needs xtr from the airfoil data or a stated assumption.

questions.question: An invented wing has a reference area of 200 ft², of which the fuselage covers 20 ft². What wetted area does the first-pass formula 2(1.02)Sexposed give?
options: 367 ft²
408 ft²
184 ft²
204 ft²
questions.explanation: The exposed area is 200 − 20 = 180 ft², and both surfaces are wetted: 2 × 1.02 × 180 = 367 ft². The full reference area would count the part the fuselage covers.

questions.question: A team takes the wing-alone span efficiency from theory, e = 1/(1 + δ), and uses it in the polar of the whole aircraft. What is the effect?
options: Induced drag is underpredicted: the whole-aircraft e is lower
Induced drag is overpredicted: the whole-aircraft e is higher
Parasite drag is underpredicted: e also scales CDmin
Induced drag is unchanged: K depends on AR only
questions.explanation: For the wing alone δ is small and e is close to 1, while 0.70 to 0.85 is typical for the whole aircraft. A higher e gives a lower K = 1/(π AR e) and too little induced drag.

questions.question: An invented aircraft flies level at CL = 0.15 with a polar that is parabolic up to a break CL of 0.5. What does the parabola give for the drag in a sustained turn at a load factor of 4, at the same speed and altitude?
options: Too little drag: CL = 0.60 is above the break
The right drag: the parabola holds up to CLmax
The right drag: CL stays at 0.15 at the same speed
Too much drag: separation above the break lowers the drag
questions.explanation: CL = n W/(q S) = 4 × 0.15 = 0.60. Above the break CL, separation adds drag, so the parabola underpredicts the thrust the sustained turn needs.

questions.question: The landing polar is built from the cruise polar. Which changes does it need?
options: Gear and flaps add CD0, and the span efficiency changes
Gear and flaps add CD0, and K keeps its cruise value
Flaps raise CLmax, and the drag stays on the cruise polar
Gear adds CD0, and flaps lower the drag at every CL
questions.explanation: Gear and flaps add CD0, and the span efficiency changes with the flap setting, so K changes too. Flaps raise the minimum drag and move it toward a higher CL; a constant added to the cruise polar misses both effects.

questions.section: Solvers agree on lift, not on drag
questions.question: On one wing and tail, three solvers agree on lift within about 1% at α = 5° but differ in drag by up to 18%. What does that mean for a drag model?
options: Validate it on a known aircraft and carry a margin
Take the lowest of the three drag values as the estimate
Trust its drag once its lift matches a second solver
Average the three drag values and drop the margin
questions.explanation: Agreement on lift says nothing about drag. The drag model is validated on a known aircraft, such as the SR22 build-up, and carried with a margin.
